form: /-b/ has cognates in most, if not all, Salish languages. In the Straits group it is realized as /-ŋ/. In Tillamook it is /-w/. In all other languages, so far as I know, it is /-m/. form: Here /-b/ is a member of the constitute /-b-i-d/. This constitute follows all theme classes except those characterized by /-b/. /-b/ alone cannot occur wherever /-b-i-d/ is possible. Compare /xʷúyubid/ 'sell to him' (page 3) and /ʔúp̓bid/ 'seat self on his lap'. The structures are different. In the former, the root /xʷuyu/ never occurs without /-b/, and /xʷúyub/ does occur without /-i-d/. In the latter, the root /ʔup̓(u)/ is found with /-b/ only when /-b/ is a member of the constitute /-b-i-d/. This complementary distribution indicates that /-b/ of themes and the /-b/of /-b-i-d/ are the same.

form: Second, B1 and B2 occur in identical syntactic environments. The same is true for A1 and A2. Directive phrases expressing actor can follow both A forms but neither B1 nor B2. Pronominal particles like /čəɬ/ 'we, us' are recipients (goals) of the action in both A constructions, while they represent the actor in all B forms.

form: I tentatively conclude that /-b/ in environments 1.i - 1.iv and 2.i - 2.iii represents the same morpheme. It seems to encompass inherent qualities and medio-passive significance. The suffix {-ab} 'by means of', 2.iv, is probably etymologically related to the secondary theme suffix {-a-} plus this /-b/. However, on the basis of the different morphologic and syntactic rôle of /-b/ in environment 3, it is thought to represent a second morpheme. The component /-b/ in environment 4 seems to be historically related to this /-b/ of 3.
